content:
✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: It's a nice challenge. A lot of small details to trip up on. Great puzzle for shortest mode.
This clash is fun but too long to solve, about 10 minutes for me, now I can do it in less than 5 minutes but it was not the case at my first play.

✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: Medium difficulty, good to exercise string manipulation, iterators and regex.
The -y flag is tricky, but still, the task is doable in under 5 minutes.
Test cases are very good and cover all scenarios.

Goal
* Their corresponding values follow the order in which these arguments appear: This sentence is unclear to me. Do you mean the following constraint?

Values (non-arguments) in the command line will only appear directly after its corresponding -t/--title or --keyword arguments.

If so, please replace the original sentence with this constraint, as it's clearer. Also, this is actually a specification of the command syntax rather than a constraint.

* Currently, the statement explains what to print before explaining how the values should be modified before printing, which makes the order somewhat confusing. Consider rewriting the process using the following framework:

1. If "-y" / "-yes" is present, process every specified keyword and title.
2. Discard values that become empty.
3. Print the surviving keywords in their original order.
4. Print the surviving title after the keywords.
5. If nothing survives, print <BLANK>.

* With the above rewriting, there's no need to mention stripping leading/trailing whitespace from the output.

Constraints
* Please remove all the points under "valid"; they're unnecessary because they merely repeat specifications in the Goal section.

Cases
* "-y" appears in 4 tests, while "-yes" appears in 4 validators. Please swap the cases so that each form appears an equal number of times in the tests and the validators.

Thanks.

Hi, User123 :D
I have a suggestion/feedback for you.
Regex is super powerful but is really not too popular, at least in my experience talking to other programmers. And I see that Regex is heavily carrying your solution. My suggestion for you is to try to code a solution without Regex to understand how people that don't have this knowledge feel.
I'm saying this as a Regex addicted :P It's something that I do when I'm also working on a contribution.
If using Regex is part of your design choice, then you can ignore my comment.

Hey @jonas_melo! I did actually start with a non-regex solution :) I parsed the tokens sequentially from left to right and stored the corresponding values for the final processing and printing. I only opted for regex when trying to write the shortest possible solution. The solution you see is my best attempt within 15 minutes.

As always, let me know what your experience with this clash was, and if there are any areas of improvement. Thank you! :)
Thank you for your feedback @kayou! Which part of the clash is the hardest bit in your opinion?

it's not really hard, it's more an additions of things:
The explaination is clear but quite long 
It has 6 commands to catch, 
Remove the vowlels if needed.
Use the <BLANK> if the answer is empty.
It has a lot of test cases, it's good but take time

I may have solved it quicker if I didn't make a mistake for the vowels removing but It only takes me 2 minutes to fix it with the tests. Now I can do it in 5 minutes because I don't need to read it completly anymore and already know about my error.
I didn't reject it because all requirements for a clash a fullfilled, if it was a shortest only I may have approved it because in this case the real time limit is 15 minutes.

The updated clash looks good to me 🙂

By the way, someone left a comment on your puzzle in the forum. You might want to take a look if you haven't seen it yet 😉
Btw I love the command line theme as I'm a shell enjoyer ( the upvote is mine :) )

A scrappy non-regex solution in Python, if you're interested:

l = int(input())
line = input()
vowels = "-y" in line
line = line.split()
title = ""
keywords = []
for i, word in enumerate(line):
    if word[0] != "-" or "-y" in word:
        continue
    elif "-t" in word:
        title = line[i + 1]
        continue
    while i + 1 < len(line) and line[i + 1][0] != "-":
        keywords.append(line[i + 1])
        i += 1
if vowels:
    title = "".join(ch for ch in title if ch not in "aeiouAEIOU")
    keywords = ["".join(ch for ch in k if ch not in "aeiouAEIOU") for k in keywords]
keywords = [f"[{k}]" for k in keywords if k]
if title:
    keywords.append(title)
print(" ".join(keywords) if keywords else "<BLANK>")

Nice. I love the while loop "capturing" the for-loop index trick.
I could solve under 5 minutes and the statement and test cases are OK. You have my approval once it's ready.
